analysis: The novel's resolution balances poetic justice with realistic social outcomes.
The reconciliation of Mrs. Ferrars shows the pragmatic side of family inheritance.
Lucy Steele's final triumph through her marriage to Robert is a classic Austenian irony.
The synthesis in Marianne's marriage to Colonel Brandon represents her final maturation.
Willoughby's fate is presented as neither fully redeemed nor entirely destroyed.
The proximity and continued bond of the two sisters remains the heart of the story.
The conclusion celebrates a moderate 'cheerfulness' grounded in reality and virtue.
